description:
We are Plutonians researching the Martians of Mars! 

We are a group of highschoolers in South Florida aspiring to be engineers, physicists, and biological researchers. We are interested in researching the terrain of mars and the Martian environment. By applying our passion towards space exploration, we will grow along with human knowledge!
summary: People always ask: how do we get to Mars but once we get there, the question becomes: where do we go and how will astronauts conduct science safely and efficiently? The Mars Positioning System (MPS) answers these questions. As astronauts prepare for an EVA, they can open the MPS and plan, view, or simulate their route. Analyzing the Martian terrain, MPS prioritizes safety and creates routes and directions built to suit the astronauts’ needs. The MPS’s AI Agent named Marital helps them do this. Martial helps astronauts select and plan destinations based on their desired research and travel conditions, such as rockiness and radiation level. All routes display the conditions along the path, directing astronauts to avoid excessive altitude changes and harmful radiation, facilitating a safe Mars mission. Utilizing topographical, geophysical, optical, and radiation data creates an interactive platform that can be used on a computer, handheld device, or VR display to guide astronauts through the Martian landscape, reaching the locations necessary for the exploration and understanding of the Martian environment. Without the ability to accurately maneuver on Mars we will remain locked out of the secrets Mars has to offer, providing specificity enables progress.
details:
The Mars Positioning System is a route planner that allows astronauts to walk on Mars and safely conduct missions. Astronauts can map out routes and analyze their safety conditions based on altitude and radiation. Its adaptive software tailors it to tablets for astronauts actively on missions, big screens so teams can work collectively, and VR for realistic simulation. This project is made of three systems that share terrain, geographical, topological, and optical data: a mapping system, an AI agent, and a VR simulation.

Our mapping system allows astronauts to plan routes and suggests safer paths to follow across 7 rover landing sites, chosen based on rover data accessibility and significance to the history of Mars exploration, such as the Ares Vallis landing site of the Sojourner rover. Created routes display distance, walking time, climb, slopes, risk levels, radiation, elevation profiles, and land directions to follow from the beginning of the mission to the end. For visualization, the system can be displayed in a 2D tablet mode designed to travel with the astronaut as they carry out their Mars walk. It is also compatible with bigger monitors, with a 3D mode designed for display at future Mars space stations. The map is a grid of squares, with each square representing a data point for altitude and radiation. To create a route that prioritizes safe conditions, we use A* search, an algorithm that finds the “cheapest” path between points. Using this algorithm, the system retrieves data between the selected start and end points of the desired route and suggests a path whose altitude and radiation values reflect safer conditions (consistent/lower altitude and lower radiation doses). For the algorithm, visualization, and deployment, we used JavaScript, React, and their libraries: Vite for server deployment, Leaflet for 2D map visualization, and Three.js for the 3D terrain view. We also used Python with FastAPI for the backend, and GDAL, rasterio, pyproj, and NumPy to process NASA/USGS HiRISE elevation data into the grid. The mapping system’s logic for retrieving data from the map and creating desired paths is the central process that bridges data and functionality between our AI agent, VR simulation, and mapping system.

Safe Mars missions take careful planning, and carrying out that plan takes a team of professionals. We propose a new member of that team: Martial, an AI agent that can create routes customized to the astronaut’s safety using the mapping system, identify destinations on Mars that support astronauts in conducting their science, help with directions, and give information on routes that have already been created. This lets astronauts interact more with their plans. Having a tool that actively helps reimagine routes and points out important values in the data helps Mars missions progress significantly. The agent uses a local language model, Llama 3.2, to write its text responses. It gets its intelligence from rover drive paths and science stops from NASA MMGIS data, radiation measurements from NASA Curiosity RAD, Meta’s data through Ollama, and map data through the mapping system. To let it interact with the map, we manually wrote functions that give it skills to read and change information through the mapping system. To build it, we used Python to run Ollama, create a server that lets the user connect to the agent, and load the same terrain the mapping system uses, so the agent can call its functions to look up data and create new routes.

Our VR simulation lets astronauts turn fidelity into a tool rather than a limitation. It uses the mapping system, so astronauts can make and edit routes while seeing what it would physically look like to walk along them. With the press of a button, the astronaut is transported onto the Martian surface, with the sky above and the rough terrain beneath them built from the same elevation data the map uses. As they choose points on the in-headset map, the route is drawn as a path both on the map and across the ground in front of them. That way, they can preview hills, slopes, and hazards before ever stepping outside. It uses Three.js with WebXR to render the terrain in the browser of a Meta Quest 3 headset, and it connects to the same backend as the mapping system so routes stay in sync across all three systems.

The Mars Positioning System introduces a Martian virtual simulation tool that will benefit astronauts on a manned mission to Mars. This simulation is available in 2D for quick tablet use onboard the spacecraft when the astronauts need to visualize their planned route. More importantly, the simulation is provided in 3D for virtual reality integration, which will allow astronauts to conduct practice runs on the routes they choose beforehand and even use the VR setup as live directions for EVA missions. Such a system will greatly benefit mission logistics, as the astronauts are not following verbal or written instructions but are instead provided with a visual pathway to their destination. Martial benefits the missions by creating varying routes based on an astronaut's missions and goals, relieving the team of the need to map out or brainstorm the ideal route to a destination. It also provides directions and aid with existing routes, unique departure and destination pathways, and any parameter information that the astronauts might request or need in their missions, which improves logistical efficiency and productivity. Overall, the mapping system benefits scientific contributions by simplifying the navigation process, and it encourages interaction by allowing the astronaut team to easily access all Martian locations and travel routes.

Our project utilizes agentic AI skills, VR integration, and authentic data from the NASA JPL Mars Trek database to synthesize the most accurate depiction of the Martian surface with the toolset we were provided. From the start, the priority of this project has been, and always will be, the safety of our users. That’s why changes in altitude and active radiation along the path were taken into consideration when designing the user interface. To ensure the product's ease of use, an AI agent called Martial, built on Ollama, was customized to suit the needs of the potential EVA team. To that end, we gave Martial the ability to list data relevant to the excursion in a readable, digestible format, such as terrain risk and active radiation dose. Martial was also equipped to categorize routes based on the EVA team's data collection needs, further easing the burden on our users. The care and dedication of our team are present in every line of code, and we aspire to advance the scientific innovation that will get humanity to Mars.
